explanation:
## One register and one AND

```systemverilog
logic din_prev;

always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  if (rst) begin
    din_prev <= 1'b1;
    rise     <= 1'b0;
  end else begin
    rise     <= din & ~din_prev;
    din_prev <= din;
  end
end
```

The detection itself is `din & ~din_prev`: high now, low on the previous edge. Everything interesting is in the three details around it.

### Why `rise` is one cycle late

Because it is a register. `rise <= din & ~din_prev` computes the condition from the values before this edge and presents it after it, so the pulse appears in the cycle following the change. A combinational `assign rise = din & ~din_prev;` would produce the pulse in the same cycle — which is a different circuit, with a different timing contract, and it is not what the specification asks for.

Registering the output is usually what you want: it makes `rise` a clean, glitch-free signal that changes only just after a clock edge, which is what the next stage needs. A combinational output carries whatever glitches the logic behind it produces.

### Why both assignments can read `din_prev`

```systemverilog
rise     <= din & ~din_prev;
din_prev <= din;
```

In that order, with non-blocking assignment, both right-hand sides use the *old* `din_prev`. There is no sequence here: the two updates happen together at the end of the edge. With blocking assignment the order would matter and the first line would have to come first — and the design would depend on the order of two statements, which is exactly the class of bug non-blocking assignment exists to prevent.

### Why `din_prev` resets to 1

This is the part that looks wrong and is not.

The specification says that coming out of reset with `din` already high must not produce a pulse. If `din_prev` reset to 0, then on the first edge after reset the design would compute `1 & ~0` and fire — reporting an edge that never happened, because nothing changed; the design simply had not been watching.

Resetting `din_prev` to 1 means "assume it was already high", so a `din` that is high when reset releases looks like no change at all. A `din` that is *low* at release and then rises is detected normally, one cycle later, as it should be.

The alternative is to reset `din_prev` to `din` itself, which is equivalent here and reads less clearly. Either way the decision has to be made deliberately: the reset value of a register that holds history is a statement about what the design believes happened before it was watching.

## The three wrong designs that pass the sample testbench

**A one-shot flag.** `if (din && !fired) begin rise <= 1; fired <= 1; end` detects the first edge and then never fires again. The sample testbench has exactly one edge in it; the `two_edges` check has two.

**A combinational output.** `assign rise = din & ~din_prev;` produces the pulse one cycle early. It passes `after_reset` and `no_fall`, and fails `one_cycle_later` — which is why that check reads `rise` *after* the edge rather than before it.

**`din_prev` reset to 0.** Fires spuriously when reset releases with `din` high. The sample testbench releases reset with `din` low, so it never sees it; `reset_with_din_high` does nothing else.

## On the waveform

Put the cursor on the edge where `din` goes high and look at `rise`: it is still low. Move one clock period right and it is high; one more and it is low again. That gap of exactly one period is the specification, and it is visible rather than inferred.

Simulation only. Nothing here says the design would synthesise or meet timing.
